summary:
I developed an open-source Python tool to identify new Earth analog sites for Moon and Mars bases on the Altiplano plateau in Bolivia and Chile. The script evaluates five volcanic candidates (Pampa Luxsar, Sajama, Ollagüe, Palpana, Uturuncu) using elevation, temperature, estimated pressure, UV radiation, rock chemistry, and hail risk. It verifies ranking stability with 5,000 random weight simulations and validates the method against Licancabur, a known analog.
This solves the problem of limited, overused testing locations by giving researchers a repeatable way to find new data-backed sites.
This matters because it makes testing space equipment and procedures on Earth more realistic and affordable before missions launch.
details:
What it does and how it works. My project looks for new Earth analog sites for future Moon and Mars bases on the Altiplano plateau in Bolivia and Chile. I collected five candidate volcanic sites (Pampa Luxsar, Sajama, Ollagüe, Palpana, Uturuncu) and built a Python script that compares them. For each site it reads elevation (Copernicus DEM) and hourly temperature and convective energy (ERA5), estimates air pressure, and combines these with UV data and rock chemistry into a weighted score. It then repeats the ranking with 5,000 random weight sets to show how stable it is, and checks the method on Licancabur, a known analog.

Benefits and impact. Agencies test seals, batteries, materials and procedures on Earth before missions. Better described analog sites make this testing more realistic and cheaper. The method is open and repeatable, so anyone can add sites or change the weights.

Tools. Python (requests, pandas, numpy, matplotlib, folium), PyCharm, the Open-Meteo API for Copernicus DEM and ERA5 data, NASA OMI UV data, and the Smithsonian GVP and GEOROC databases for rock information. The slides are an .odp presentation. I used an ordinary laptop, no special hardware. [I also used an AI assistant (Claude) for research help, code drafts and slide text, and I checked the sources myself.]

Creativity. Instead of reusing famous analog sites, I used open space and Earth data to look for sites that are not listed. I added a known-analog control, a stability test, and hail as an operational stress factor.

Factors considered. No Earth site has Mars air, so pressure here is about 75 times higher than on Mars. Pressure is an estimate from the standard atmosphere. Hail is only a proxy (CAPE). A record UV value reported at Licancabur is disputed, so I mark it as such. The weights are my assumption, and the control check is only a sanity check, because the criteria resemble Licancabur. I also kept in mind access, safety and permits at 5,500–6,500 metres.
